opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a question I get a lot, and I think the honest answer is that long context changes the trade-offs, but it doesn't make retrieval or fine-tuning obsolete.

On the RAG side, long context is genuinely great for a certain class of problems. If you have a handful of documents, say a few contracts, a codebase that isn't too big, or a couple of research papers, you can often just put everything into the prompt and skip the whole retrieval pipeline. No chunking strategy, no embedding model, no vector database to maintain. That's a real simplification, and for prototyping especially I think people should try the "just stuff it in the context" approach first before building infrastructure.

But there are a few reasons retrieval sticks around. One is cost and latency. Attention still scales unfavorably with sequence length, and even with caching and the various efficiency tricks, processing hundreds of thousands of tokens on every query is expensive compared to retrieving the five most relevant passages. The second is scale. If your knowledge base is an entire company's documentation or millions of records, it simply doesn't fit, no matter how long the context gets. And third, there's the quality question. Models have gotten much better at the needle-in-a-haystack type tests, but retrieving a single fact is different from reasoning over many scattered pieces of information spread across a huge context. Performance on those harder tasks still tends to degrade as the context grows. So giving the model a focused, relevant context often just works better.

I actually think the more likely outcome is a hybrid: you retrieve more coarsely, maybe whole documents or large sections instead of tiny chunks, and then let the long-context model do the fine-grained reasoning. That makes retrieval less brittle, because you no longer need perfect chunking to succeed.

Fine-tuning is a slightly different story. I've always thought people reach for fine-tuning too quickly when what they really want is to inject knowledge. Fine-tuning isn't a very reliable way to teach a model new facts; it's better at changing behavior, like style, format, following a domain-specific task structure, or being more concise. Long context makes that distinction even clearer. If the goal is "the model should know what's in these documents," then putting the documents in context or retrieving them is usually the better approach, and it's easier to update when the documents change. Fine-tuning still makes sense when you want consistent behavior without a huge prompt every time, when you want a smaller, cheaper model to perform well on a narrow task, or when you need the model to adopt patterns that are hard to describe in instructions.

So my summary would be this: long context lowers the barrier to entry and removes a lot of the engineering pain for small and medium-sized problems, but retrieval remains important for scale and efficiency, and fine-tuning remains important for behavior and specialization. They're complementary tools rather than competitors.

r001.rationale: It says that processing a very large knowledge base on every query is expensive compared with retrieving a few relevant passages, identifying large collections and repeated queries as a setting where RAG remains useful.

r002.rationale: It says that when the goal is for the model to know what documents contain, putting them in context is usually better than fine-tuning.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says that for a handful of documents, putting everything in the prompt can let you skip the retrieval pipeline.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and it's one I get asked a lot because the context windows have grown so dramatically. A couple of years ago we were excited about 4k or 8k tokens, and now we're routinely seeing a million tokens or more. So the natural question is, if I can just paste my entire document collection into the prompt, why would I bother with retrieval or with fine-tuning?

I think the honest answer is that long context reduces the need in some cases, but it doesn't eliminate it, and the reasons are mostly practical rather than theoretical.

Let me start with RAG. The first thing is cost and latency. Even if a model can technically handle a million tokens, you're paying for all of those tokens on every single query, and the attention computation scales with the context length. So if you have a corpus of a few hundred documents and you're answering thousands of questions a day, stuffing everything into the context every time is just an enormous waste compared to retrieving the three or four relevant chunks. Prompt caching helps with this, but it doesn't make the problem go away entirely.

The second thing is that long context and accurate use of long context are not the same thing. We've all seen the "needle in a haystack" benchmarks, and the models have gotten much better at those. But those tests are kind of easy, right? You're looking for one very distinctive sentence. When you look at harder evaluations, where the model has to reason over multiple pieces of information scattered throughout the context, or where there's a lot of distracting, similar-looking content, performance still degrades as the context grows. So retrieval is also acting as a kind of focusing mechanism. You're pre-filtering so the model is reasoning over relevant information rather than being distracted by irrelevant information.

And then there's the dynamic data aspect. If your knowledge base changes every hour, you're going to re-index and retrieve anyway. The long context doesn't really help you with freshness.

Where I do think long context changes things is that it makes RAG more forgiving. You no longer have to be surgical about chunking and retrieving exactly the right 500 tokens. You can retrieve more generously, pull in whole sections or whole documents, and let the model sort it out. So the retrieval system can be simpler and less brittle. I'd say long context makes RAG easier rather than making it obsolete.

Now, fine-tuning on documents is a bit of a different story, and here I'd actually say the case has gotten weaker for a specific use case, which is knowledge injection. There was a period where people thought, I'll fine-tune the model on my company's documents and then it will "know" them. And in my experience that works poorly. Models are surprisingly bad at absorbing new factual knowledge through a small amount of fine-tuning. They tend to either not learn the facts reliably or they learn the style of the documents but hallucinate the details. For that use case, retrieval or just putting the documents into context is almost always better, and long context makes it even more attractive.

But I don't think fine-tuning is going away, because it's good at other things. It's good at teaching a model a format, a style, a particular way of behaving. It's good for specialized tasks where you have a lot of labeled examples and you want a smaller, cheaper model to do one thing well. And instruction tuning and preference tuning are obviously not replaced by long context at all. So I'd distinguish between fine-tuning for knowledge, where I'm skeptical, and fine-tuning for behavior or skills, where I think it remains very relevant, especially if you care about running something small and local.

So if I had to summarize, I'd say in practice most systems I see end up being a combination. You use a long-context model, you still retrieve so you're not paying for and distracting the model with irrelevant stuff, and you fine-tune when you need a specific behavior or want to compress a capability into a smaller model. The context window growing just shifts the boundaries a bit. It doesn't collapse the whole stack into one technique.

r001.rationale: It describes answering thousands of questions over a corpus of a few hundred documents and says retrieving a few relevant chunks avoids repeatedly supplying the whole collection.

r002.rationale: For knowledge injection, it says retrieval or putting documents into context is almost always better than fine-tuning, making document fine-tuning unnecessary for that use case.

r003.rationale: It discusses pasting the collection into context as an alternative, but concludes that long context makes RAG easier rather than obsolete and recommends continuing to retrieve. It does not clearly state that context can make retrieval unnecessary for those documents.

astra-6.text:
I think long context changes the trade-offs, but it doesn’t make retrieval or fine-tuning obsolete. They solve somewhat different problems.

If you have a few documents and they fit in the context window, putting them directly into the prompt can be a very convenient approach. You don’t have to build a retrieval pipeline or worry about whether the retriever missed a relevant passage. But fitting information into the context window doesn’t necessarily mean the model will use all of it reliably. And processing a lot of context can still have a cost in terms of latency and computation.

With RAG, you’re selecting the information that’s relevant to a particular question. That remains useful when you have a large collection of documents or information that changes frequently. You can update the documents without retraining the model. And longer context can help RAG, too—you can retrieve more complete passages instead of squeezing everything into tiny chunks.

Fine-tuning is a different lever. I’d generally use it to teach the model how to perform a task—how to respond, follow a particular format, or work with domain-specific examples—rather than treat it as a reliable way to store documents. If you need an exact fact from a document, providing that document at inference time is usually a more direct approach.

So I see these as complementary. Longer context makes some applications simpler, retrieval helps select the right information, and fine-tuning helps shape what the model does with that information.

r001.rationale: The response says RAG remains useful for a large or frequently changing collection, but does not identify repeated use of a fixed collection.

r002.rationale: It describes direct prompting and says fine-tuning is not a reliable way to store documents, but does not state that providing documents in context can replace fine-tuning on them.

r003.rationale: It says that when a few documents fit in context, they can be placed directly in the prompt, so there is no need to build a retrieval pipeline.

sol-6.1.text:
I think long context changes the trade-offs, but it doesn’t eliminate the need for retrieval or fine-tuning. They solve somewhat different problems.

If you have a handful of documents and they fit into the context window, putting them directly into the prompt can be a very practical approach. You don’t have to build a retrieval pipeline. But fitting the information into the context window doesn’t necessarily mean the model will use all of it reliably. And there’s still the cost and latency of processing that context.

Retrieval is useful when you have a large collection, when the information changes frequently, or when you want to identify the sources behind an answer. Long context can make retrieval more flexible: you can retrieve larger sections and worry less about cutting out the surrounding information.

Fine-tuning, I would think of more as teaching the model how to perform a task—how to respond, what format to use, or how to handle domain-specific examples. You can train on documents, but I wouldn’t assume that turns the model into a reliable database of everything in those documents.

So I see these as complementary. You might fine-tune for the behavior you want, retrieve the relevant information, and use a longer context window to give the model enough material to work with.

r001.rationale: The response says retrieval is useful for a large collection, but does not identify repeated use of a fixed collection as the setting.

r002.rationale: It describes direct prompting for documents that fit, but does not say this can eliminate fine-tuning on those documents.

r003.rationale: It says that when a handful of documents fit in the context window, using them directly can avoid building a retrieval pipeline.
